blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData sells proxies the way prepaid phone plans sell minutes: one flat $1/GB balance that works across residential, mobile and datacenter pools. Static residential IPs start at $1.79 each in monthly bundles (20 for $49) with unlimited bandwidth. It is one of the cheapest ways into residential traffic, but it is a newer brand with less independent benchmarking than the established names.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
Webshare in 2026: what you get

Webshare is the self-service favourite of solo developers. It gives away 10 shared datacenter proxies with 1 GB a month forever, sells paid datacenter lists from $2.99 for 100 proxies, and offers static ISP and rotating residential networks with a clean dashboard and good API. Its rotating residential pool is listed at 80M+ IPs in 195 countries, with sticky sessions from one minute to 24 hours. The main catch is that monthly bandwidth resets every 30 days and does not roll over.

Strengths: Permanent free datacenter plan for testing; Low, transparent residential pricing; Excellent dashboard and API; Sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Weak spots: Bandwidth resets monthly with no rollover; No mobile proxies; 500-request default concurrency limit.
Pricing: FloppyData vs Webshare

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

Webshare's rotating residential plans cost $3.50 for 1 GB, $27.50 for 10 GB, $65 for 25 GB, $225 for 100 GB and $875 for 500 GB per month, falling to $1.40/GB at 3 TB. Yearly billing is about 30% cheaper but is paid upfront for a 360-day term. Unused bandwidth resets every 30 days.

At 10 GB a month, FloppyData is the cheaper option at about $10 against $27.50 for Webshare, roughly 64% less. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $100 with FloppyData and $225 with Webshare: a 56% saving in FloppyData's favour. Both FloppyData and Webshare work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and Webshare lists '80M+'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and Webshare lists 195. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while Webshare offers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and Webshare offers rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: Webshare. Webshare has the edge here. Why: low prices and a developer-friendly API. How FloppyData compares: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. FloppyData: workable for light tasks. Webshare: fine for light rank tracking. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With FloppyData: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. With Webshare: 24-hour sticky sessions and cheap static ISP IPs. Run the same small test on both before committing.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. FloppyData: city targeting at a flat rate. Webshare: good for US work with ZIP targeting, thinner elsewhere. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Ad verification and geo-testing: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With FloppyData: limited targeting depth and published data. With Webshare: no mobile network and limited selector combinations. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Tight budgets: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. FloppyData: a flat $1/GB on any volume. Webshare: free tier plus some of the lowest per-GB rates here. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. Webshare: ID checks only when flagged or for restricted categories. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and Webshare before you commit
The quickest way to choose between FloppyData and Webshare is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 0, Webshare in 1, and 5 are ties. That makes Webshare the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while Webshare is strongest for solo developers and small teams. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
